lines.text: What if you could turn invisible —
but only while holding your breath?
Mom is holding your math test.
The spot where you were standing …
Nobody knows why she opens the fridge.
Staring right at where you're standing.
Mom doesn't punish you for the three.
She punishes you for scaring her half to death.
Hold your breath, and you disappear.
Your clothes, your sandals, the bag in your hand — gone too.
Breathe out — even a little — and you're back.
And talking? Talking is breathing out.
While you're invisible, you can't say a word.
most people can hold their breath for about thirty seconds to a minute.
And that urge to breathe? It's not from running out of oxygen.
It's carbon dioxide building up in your blood.
Your body screams long before you're actually in danger.
About forty seconds at a time.
First, you have to relearn everything.
You're invisible behind your classmate Huy when he drops his snack — and you laugh.
Like Lunar New Year string lights.
Only one person is never fooled.
Hide and seek: you stand invisible in the middle of the living room.
Bin covers his eyes, counts to ten.
You hold your breath really loud.
The family altar is loaded with fruit, sweet rice cakes, dessert.
Mom lights three more incense sticks.
Grandma and Grandpa came to eat.
You decide you will never, ever tell her.
You sneak into the teachers' office.
The literature exam is sitting right on the desk.
Question three is way too long.
Three days of cleaning the school toilets.
when your face touches cold water, your body flips on something called the diving reflex.
You can hold your breath longer.
So every morning, you dunk your face in a bowl of ice water.
Mom thinks it's a skincare routine.
The world record for holding your breath is over eleven minutes.
And for you, three minutes is enough to do …
Then the rumors start at school.
A door opening by itself in the hallway.
A sandwich vanishing from a cafeteria tray.
A team of ghost hunters shows up with an energy meter.
You're standing right next to them.
When you're invisible, you hear what people say when they think you're not there.
Your friends are planning a weekend hangout.
Doesn't really matter if he comes or not.
But for the first time, you wish you didn't have to come back.
And something strange starts to happen.
Even when you're breathing — people don't see you.
On your birthday, the group chat stays silent all day.
That night, Bin climbs into your bed, lies down next to you.
Were you holding your breath all day?
Star lanterns, carp lanterns, spinning lanterns.
A lantern in one hand, your brother in the other.
A man in a baseball cap, carrying Bin toward the end of the street.
His voice is lost in the drums.
Nobody can stop what they can't see.
Reaches the end of the street.
A motorbike is waiting, engine running.
It feels like someone is sitting on your chest.
The edges of your vision start going dark.
But alone, you can't stop a grown man and a motorbike.
And for this street to see you — you have to do the one thing you've been avoiding for months.
In the middle of the street.
And for the first time in months — everyone is looking at you.
The lantern seller steps in front of the bike.
Two motorbike taxi drivers grab the man's arms.
A woman selling grilled corn scoops Bin up.
Five minutes later, the police arrive.
I heard you holding your breath.
You sit down on the curb.
Your friends ask if you're free this weekend.
One breath is all it takes.
Letting people see you is the hard part.
The plate of rice cakes on the altar is half empty.
Looks at the crumbs on your hoodie.
Grandma and Grandpa came to eat again?
That night, Bin climbs into your bed.
Puts his ear on your chest.
So — if you could turn invisible for three minutes, what would you do first?
Hit like and subscribe for more "what ifs."
